items.body: Ambrose Akinmusire and Mary Halvorson – Slo-Mo Neon Luminate Hoverings (Nonesuch) Slo-Mo Neon Luminate Hoverings is the first recorded collaboration by the duo of trumpeter Ambrose Akinmusire and guitarist Mary Halvorson. Spontaneity and through composed material are on display, with both playing roles in all of the pieces. “Prelude in the Ash” begins with a questing trumpet solo before the guitar joins with a sinuous arpeggiated chord pattern. “This Vivid” is more muscular, with solo material – a high trumpet note and single line guitar solos – repeated amid ebullient shouts. Calling a piece “Soundcheck” might suggest something off the cuff, but there is a seamless give and take between Akinmusire and Halvorson, and electronics augment their sonic palette. “Soundcheck” ends with a skittering, web-like pattern. Conversely, “Blood and Sand” is a fetching ballad, with a captivating chord progression underlaying a supple trumpet solo. “Nice to Meet You Again for the First Time” begins with an angular yet nimble guitar solo. Akinmusire joins, doubling the intricate melody and then veering off in cascading runs. The two diverge into separate free play, always coming back to the core melody only then to return to a cat and mouse game of call and response. Likewise, “Watersmoke” begins with a melody played in unison which periodically returns, interspersed with atmospheric interludes. Akinmusire explores the altissimo register in solos on “Tangled Pretty,” returning to earth to join Halvorson, who plays arpeggiations but also explores pitch bends and rapid shifts in register. The two revel in spicy dissonant verticals in the opening of “Ofo,” only to have the piece unfold into a lyrical melody. However, Halvorson keeps some of the tension of the previous section in her playing, employing dynamic shifts and glissandos to good effect. In the last passage of the piece, Akinmusire plays extended high notes yet still executes a seamless fadeout with Halvorson. The title track, also its longest at around eight minutes in duration, closes the album. It is nice to hear them stretch out a bit. “Slo-Mo Neon Luminate Hoverings” opens with a lyrical melody from Akinmusire and delicately strummed chords from Halvorson. She gradually moves in sync with the trumpeter, doubling the melody. Washes of keening looped harmonies create oasis-like interludes between repetitions of “Slo-Mo Neon’s” main theme, and populate the piece’s lustrous long denouement. Akinmusire and Halvorson are both gifted soloists, which is abundantly demonstrated on Slo-Mo Neon. But it is their work in tandem that is most memorable. Dare we hope that this pairing continues to perform and record together? -Christian Carey   The post Ambrose Akinmusire and Mary Halvorson (Recording Review) appeared first on Sequenza21.
items._cn_summary: 这是小号手Ambrose Akinmusire与吉他手Mary Halvorson的首次录音合作专辑。两位音乐家在即兴演奏与预先谱写的素材之间自由穿梭，每首曲目都展现两人对等的声音角色。作品跨越抒情旋律、尖锐不协和音、自由对话与电子音效增强等多种语汇：小号在高音区探索极限，吉他在琶音、弯音与快速变位中延展音色。两人常以齐奏旋律开始，渐次分叉为各自即兴的追逐游戏，再回归核心主题。电子元素的介入扩展了原生音色，回路化的和声层构建出抽象间隔。最长曲目标题曲让两人得以充分展开，旋律与循环和声彼此缠绕，尾声绵长。整体显示两位独奏家各自的实力，更突出他们在互动中产生的化学反应。

items.body: From a round-the-world bicycle trip, instrument maker and field recordist Sam Underwood reflects on the ways in which his long journey and changing environment alters his practice Some years ago, I recorded an album titled Field Augmentation with my friend and collaborator David Morton. The record was made by introducing recorded sounds into an existing soundscape through a battery-powered amplifier. The final pieces are field recordings of these ‘augmented soundscapes’ in which post-production is limited to topping and tailing, adjusting levels and equalisation. It was released by [RHP] CDRs and promptly disappeared without trace, but the premise never did. It has quietly shaped how I listen and how I record, in the studio and in the field, ever since. Over time I have realised that the moments that bring me the greatest joy are rarely the ones I intended to capture. An off-kilter clanking due to a loose component on one of my musical machines, a passing motorcyclist’s whoop whoop cutting through a carefully framed recording, my stomach rumbling as I rest my recorder on the only available relatively flat surface in my tent – these intrusions often add life to the material I set out to document. Yet my recording habits tend to conspire against such occurrences. When field recording I still find myself seeking out quiet refuges from the mechanised world, spaces where I can isolate what has caught my ear. Those recordings say as much about that ear – its preferences, its blind spots – as they do about the places themselves. A more honest portrait of recent soundscapes would feature dense birdsong modulated by multiple air-conditioning units, distributed multichannel TikTok hellscapes, or just loads of human bustle. To some degree, the recordings gathered on Bimbling By Bike – Year One in field recordings lean more towards these de facto soundscapes. The release collects 20 pieces from the first year of a cycle tour that has thus far seen us ride from the UK to Guinea-Bissau. It also includes a single Field Augmentation work that will later appear on a new iteration of the series for release on Graham Dunning’s Fractal Meat Cuts label. As with the tour itself, the material is conditioned by whatever my attention, energy levels and surroundings would accommodate at the time. Crossing the Sahara by bicycle, for instance, left both me and my microphones overwhelmed: wind, sand and fatigue limited what was possible. That feels less like a loss now than part of the practice. One of our touring mantras is that every route chosen, by its nature, features a series of omissions. Riding one way means not riding another. The same applies to recording. A second shift in my approach has come from embracing transience. Before this tour I worked in a workshop full of tools, with part finished instruments in every corner and a sense that many were being developed and used as long term projects. On the road I have a few basic hand tools and no capacity to store or transport substantial objects. Instruments are improvised, used in a Field Augmentation piece, then given away. I’ve even taken to making some rudimentary sonic graffiti pieces again (a project that always embraced impermanence) from discarded items we happen across. I’ve also been reading about traditional instruments from the regions we pass through. Early in the journey, in northern Spain, I came across the Basque sunprinu (or sunpriñu), a double reed aerophone made entirely – reed and all – from a single strip of bark harvested within a narrow seasonal window, which then fails as it dries out. From that point on, I have fully embraced the never-to-again-occur circumstances and ephemerality that seem especially central to my current lifestyle. This also builds well on the unwritten Field Augmentation rule that, failing major disruptions to the recording, the first take is the only take. Get it done, and move on. After all, that’s the take you were going to end up choosing anyway! Carrying the extra weight of recording gear and instrument making tools on a long cycle tour is not always an obvious decision. At times, I’ve wondered why I persist. The answer, for now, is that these activities remain central to my sense of who I am, something I confronted quite directly in a mini identity crisis after leaving everything behind. I’m not pursuing profile or career advancement through this work; I am, however, attached to practices that help me make sense of moving through the world. Instead of lamenting the facilities I no longer have, I’ve started to appreciate what the road affords. One unexpected discovery is how well the bicycle functions as a recording platform. Over 12 months we’ve moved through the UK, Denmark, Norway, Germany, France, Spain, Morocco, Mauritania, Senegal and Guinea-Bissau. The pace is fast enough to cover distance yet slow and porous enough to remain embedded in the local soundscape – in conversation with people, weather, nature, infrastructure. This has enabled encounters with, among other things, the UK’s Time & Tide bells, the distinct sonic effect of a pair of tunnels at a former Spanish salt-drying facility, and the vast iron ore train in Mauritania, all in a way that flying over or speeding past them in a car wouldn’t have facilitated. In retrospect, I wish I had treated my prior everyday cycling in the same way: commutes, rides to the shops, neighbourhood Bike Bus journeys all now strike me as missed recording opportunities. The other aspect I love about travelling by bicycle is how shifts in the sonic environment are slow and visceral. Like a world-record-breaking longest crossfade. Your ear is rarely dumped into an unfamiliar sonic environment, it has to make its way there, as if listening to an extreme time-stretched version of the world, where (sights and) sounds are telegraphed long prior to becoming fully present in the soundscape. It’s a magical experience. As we move into our second year on the road, with Japan as a distant co-ordinate, I expect the recording practice to keep mutating. Compiling this release has already nudged my focus towards sounds that more clearly situate the listener in a specific region. Not site specific in a narrow sense, but attentive to languages, birdsong and other phenomena that give a rough impression of place. I also want to further loosen my resistance to sounds less favoured, to allow noise to remain rather than treat it as a contaminant. It’s strange that in my wider practice I have always been sanguine about such sounds, but as soon as I put my field recording hat on, I deem these sounds to be avoided. Lately, I have also been reflecting on Finlay-Walsh’s proposals around first-person field recording, which is present in some of these first year recordings, but I plan to elevate in my future recordings. And then there is Field Augmentation, which continues to rely on actively altering the soundscape as it is recorded, and I expect those pieces to proliferate as we travel. If there is an overarching aim emerging from all this, it is to retrain my field recordist’s ear: to notice what it has learnt to avoid or filter out, and to let that into the work.
items._genre: field recording / sound art / experimental ambient / electroacoustic
items._cn_summary: 文章围绕乐器制作者兼野外录音师Sam Underwood的骑行录音项目展开。他在自行车环球之旅中收集声音素材，从英国一路骑行至几内亚比绍，途经撒哈拉沙漠等地，将沿途的环境声响汇编成《Bimbling By Bike – Year One》。作品延续其早期Field Augmentation理念，将录制的声音通过电池供电放大器引入现有声景，后期仅做修剪与均衡处理。录音并非刻意寻找的宁静角落，而是拥抱真实的环境：鸟鸣与空调共鸣、社交媒体声浪与人声嘈杂交织。Underwood反思了录音习惯中的主观偏好与盲点，认为每段路线都意味着另一段路线的缺席，录音亦如此。骑行中身体的疲劳、设备的局限、风的干扰都成为实践的一部分。整张专辑是关于声景、注意力与移动的诚实记录，发行于小众厂牌，声音素材真实而未经过度雕琢。

items.body: The most adventurous music offers an exchange with its listeners. Dedicate time and attention to its often unpredictable operations, and receive a return. For me, when I listen to The Giant is Awkward , the latest release from Victor Vieira-Branco’s trio Bark Culture, the return is as immediate as it is sustained. A feeling of something like exhilaration in the moment, of following master improvisers on their way to a circuitous but directing truth. Victor Vieira-Branco is a vibraphonist and composer who grew up in Brazil, but spends most of his time these days in Philadelphia, that is when he is not touring with Rob Mazurek’s Exploding Star Orchestra or Chad Taylor’s Quintet, which played Big Ears this March. With The Giant , his trio Bark Culture has its second release, the maiden voyage being the acclaimed Warm Wisdom from 2024, and is rounded out by bassist John Moran and drummer Joey Sullivan. Together, the trio makes music that is angular, surprising, and almost always just off center. The opening track, “Palace,” is a representative example of this. After a slanted theme marked by what sounds like finger pounding by vibes and piano, the music descends into a deep madness with Sullivan and Moran following no particular time or engaging in any semblance of functional harmony. But after several minutes of gleefully wild chaos, the band unifies again, rights itself, and collectively enters a second set of thematic material before leaping into yet one more wall of noise. I should pause to state that this release is made particularly special by the presence of guest pianist Sam Yulsman. Yulsman is one of the engines behind the supreme madness one finds on this album, as he smashes and mashes and slams his piano keys in the sections I find to be most adventurous, most dissonant and wild. He even contributed a composition, the second song “Farce,” which, with its asymmetrical thematic unison of vibes and piano leading into surrounded moments of unhinged sonic rantings, is right at home on The Giant is Awkward . Vieira-Branco is composer of all of the other works here. While his compositions are lovely, the interplay of the musicians is what makes this album move from coherent to something really special. Drummer Joey Sullivan seems to me to have a particularly strong musical relationship with Vieira-Branco, and the two are as likely to play their respective percussion instruments with mathematical precision as they are to respond spontaneously to sudden snare rolls, cymbal crashes, or introverted vibraphone bowing. And all of this is not to suggest Victor V-B’s compositions are not at times stunningly beautiful. Listen, for example, to the penultimate work on the record, “Panic.” The piece is quiet, introspective, full of tenderness and empathy and, in communicating as much, is not at all what I expect when I think of the word panic . The song seems almost guru-like in this way as it flows in and out of time and traditional harmonies to moments of collective improvisation. Panic is a navigable state here, as marked by beauty as it is by its unexpected torsions, but always as composed and improvised as the day itself. The Giant is Awkward is one of the standout releases of this year for me. Its depth of feeling and spontaneously combustible surprises find themselves one minute collectedly astute, and beard grabbing lunatic raving the next. For all of this work’s intelligence and its musicians technical virtuosity, there is never a moment where I feel the energy is not in service of art or the music itself. And this is the adventure Bark Culture has offered to its potential listeners with this album: follow them with attention and effort, and deep pleasure manifests along the path with wisps of transformation sailing in its sonic wilderness. The Giant is Awkward can be found here . The Giant is Awkward by Victor Vieira-Branco's Bark Culture Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这是Victor Vieira-Branco三重奏Bark Culture的第二张专辑，由颤音琴手领衔，携手贝斯手John Moran和鼓手Joey Sullivan，并邀请钢琴手Sam Yulsman担任特邀。乐评指出，作品呈现出棱角分明、出人意料且常偏离中心的特质——开篇曲《Palace》以倾斜的主题开场，随坠入近乎无调性的狂野混沌，几分钟后乐队重新统一，进入第二组主题材料后又跃入另一片噪音之墙。Yulsman的钢琴是这场混乱的核心引擎，其作《Farce》以不对称的主题齐奏引领，衔接失控般的声响宣泄。整张专辑在精准与自发性之间游走：数学般的打击精确度与即兴的小军鼓滚奏、镲片爆裂、颤音琴弓弦内省交织。倒数第二首《Panic》则以安静、内省、充满温柔与同理心的姿态展开，与标题形成反讽，在时间与传统和声之外自由流转，形成整张专辑的情感平衡点。

items.body: Review by kev rowland — 'Fractal Guitar 4' is the fourth instalment in the 'Fractal Guitar' series which Swiss composer and guitarist Stephan Thelen initiated in 2015, with the last chapter being released in 2022. This is not the only series he has been working on and along with separate projects this is his 13th release since the first, which in itself was his 12th solo album outside of his work with Sonar. On this he again has multiple guests, many of whom he has worked with before, with only Norwegian guitarist Eivind Aarset playing on every track alongside Thelen, with the others contributing here and there. These include American guitarist Jon Durant, Israeli drummer Yogev Gabay, Markus Reuter from Germany (touch guitar), Fabio Anile from Italy (electric piano), Stefan Huth from Germany (touch bass guitar), Giri Subramaniam from India (tabla) and Andi Pupato from Switzerland (percussion), so a truly international line-up.When I started listening to this the first person I thought of was Allan Holdsworth, and that stayed true through the whole album although at times I also thought of John McLaughlin. One thing I found fascinating in that of all those involved, including Thelen himself, the musician I listen to most is Markus Reuter in multiple projects, yet here he is playing a role as opposed to driving music in his own manner, so his distinctive style is somewhat subsumed into the whole. One of the things which is fascinating with this album are the time signatures and polyrhythms being used, where musicians can actually be placing different signatures against each other which should lead to chaos both in the studio and in the brain but somehow it works, and I have no logical explanation as to why.If Gabriel was a guitarist as opposed to a singer I could imagine some of his early 80's albums sounding something like this, while King Crimson fans will also discover plenty here to enjoy as this is hugely complex and complicated, a music theorist's wet dream, yet there is also a clarity which makes it enjoyable as opposed to a chore. I cannot say this is overly easy to listen to, and is not for everyone, but if you want to hike through the pass less travelled you will find much more beauty than those who stay on the highways.
items._cn_summary: 这是瑞士吉他手与作曲家Stephan Thelen「分形吉他」系列的第四部作品，延续自2015年开始的创作脉络。整张专辑以吉他为核心，邀请挪威吉他手Eivind Aarset参与全部曲目，其余九位来自美国、以色列、德国、意大利、瑞士、印度等地的音乐人则各自贡献段落，形成高度国际化的阵容。Thelen大量运用复合节奏与多变拍号，让乐手在不同的节拍框架中叠加演奏，评论者形容其本应造成混乱，却在实际听感中获得了异常的清晰与统一。马克斯·鲁特的触弦吉他在其中收敛了个性以融入整体框架。专辑将霍兹沃思式的液态连复段、麦劳林的东方神秘感、Gabriel早期的艺术摇滚气质与King Crimson式的复杂结构融为一体，虽不以平易近人为目标，却为愿意深入探究的听者提供了丰富的层次与智识快感。

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.

items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz联合作曲家Francesco Paolo Paladino与诗人Luca Chino Ferrari推出专辑《Songs of Compassion》，收录十一首颠覆传统歌曲形式的实验作品。音乐以钢琴为核心，叠加弦乐、木管与合成器音层，采用非线性和调式手法，打破西方和声运动的惯性思维，呈现出类似Steve Reich与Philip Glass的极简重复与相位偏移美学。Moskowitz的演唱如同方法派演员，将哲思歌词娓娓道来，旋律随意识流动而非遵循功能和声。歌词延续1960年代抗议歌曲传统，《Pale Wanderer》剖析极权主义的合谋机制，《Charlottesville》直面新纳粹集会事件，同时包含对死亡与宇宙位置的沉思。整张专辑诞生于与1960年代相似的政治分裂时刻，以高远而真诚的姿态将先锋音乐与社会批判融为一体。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: Di Mashin ?? ?????? by Maria Ka I n the High Middle Ages, Hildegard of Bingen said that �The truly holy person welcomes all that is earthly.� William Blake declared in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790) that �Exuberance is beauty.� In 1855, Walt Whitman published the poem �Song Of Myself, 51� in Leaves of Grass , which contains the famous line �I am large, I contain multitudes.� I�m just skimming the surface of mystical experience, of those struck by wonder and an all-encompassing insight into how people fit into the �grand scheme of things.� At some point on this trajectory, the boundary between the religious and the secular breaks down and simply being human becomes the ultimate wow. Which brings us to Polish artist Maria Ka�s latest album Di Mashin . Ka found that her family had Jewish roots, a discovery that led her to an immersion in Jewish studies and the Yiddish language. As on 2023�s Der Hemshekh , she unreels original songs written in Yiddish, embracing a politically active feminism and a committed meta-universality. Her musical vision is fragrantly mystical, and she presents us with a whole Yiddish cosmos. While not sharing the same type of musical style, Ka reminds me of John Zorn�s aesthetic of mixing the grotesque and the sacred into Jewish experimental music. She also reminds me of the woman on the phone sampled on Wally Brill�s Jewish cantorial electronica album The Covenant (2007), who confesses she can�t sleep after hearing someone in a bar talking about the Book of Ezekiel and being haunted by the vision of Jews arriving from a future space-time. She sees that we are all suspended in webs of relationships. She is also deeply aware of how we are subject to larger social forces and structures � which sometimes must be met with radical action -- that are the machinery of life. There is a heavy dose of electro and punkish attitude spinning through her musical universe. Ostensibly, the album is divided between electronic and rock tracks, but there is a consistency to the sound that is united in loopy joy. At its best, Di Mashin is sly and sexy. Opening track �Alef � Tsentauri Disko� finds Ka in the city, musing on the seaside, wriggling like a snake at night, and watching Gdańsk wake up. �I often Dream about Cosmos, about the Land above the Earth / overhead / Alef Centauri Jewish disco!� she sings, set to a thumping urban electro grind. (See video below) Di Mashin ?? ?????? by Maria Ka �Vos iz dos?� is a standout, more in the �rock� vein, with Ka howling a debate over the Yiddish language itself. Perhaps it is based in a critique that she received, as she starts with What is this? Maria, what is this? I constantly hear it, it has not finished You speak no Yiddish!/ It�s so easy! Your language is incorrect, mistaken is your speech and dialect! � Given that Ka is producing new modern songs in Yiddish, there is something disarming in acknowledging the tension over who might claim ownership of language itself. Di Mashin ?? ?????? by Maria Ka �SuperNove� might remind listeners of Jacob wrestling with God, if that battle was done to an �80s new wave beat. Ka has visions of the past, the Old World and old demons, and she fights a ghost that rises to block her way: � I fought him with Strength, punched him with my both hands�I triumphed over him! I myself � I did triumph over him! � And after that victory, � it�s a great Surprise � the Past melted in the Cosmic Blast! � Ka also seems to be challenging herself, pointing in new directions. �Di Kosmish motorn (Cosmic engines)� brought to mind the former Warsaw Village Band�s blues-influenced singer Maja Kleszcz. Depeche Mode�s (fronted by Dave Gahan, of Jewish ancestry) forays into fusing electronica with blues might be another touchpoint. Hearing the cosmic engines like a modern day Pythagoras, she is awestruck by hearing the cosmic engines in her head. �Dos geverk (The mechanism)� offers some grinding guitars to convey the constant motion of the daily rat race � echoed later on by the title track, �Di Mashin (The Machine),� which peels back the layers of society to reveal the incessant obsession for money. The music of �The Machine� is hyperspeed cabaret, close to madness. The system demands more money � but she indicates that she is a spanner in the works, working to bring it down: � I watch the machine�s death / Full and steadily red is my hand in the end. � Di Mashin ?? ?????? by Maria Ka Feminist politics come to the fore on �Ikh bin a froy (I am a woman),� and Ka reminds me a bit of the divine Ms. H of Bingen chanting over a motoric beat. She refuses to be hemmed in by structures, signaling that the Forest is her home, the stars her friends; �I wake up every day / and new scroll create.� Album closer �Di milkhome� (War)� is more future blues, transposing war, empty shipyards, and advice from her mother that all miseries will end and freedom will navigate the turmoil �like huge ships at Sea.� Di Mashin is possessed by such a singular offbeat vision and personal mythology that I wonder where Maria Ka will take her Yiddishfuturism next�Perhaps beyond our solar system, grooving on an interstellar plane with her band wriggling like snakes. Find the artist online. Further listening: Maria Ka - Der Hemshekh Warsaw Village Band & Bassałyki - Sploty WoWaKin - Kraj za miastem

items._cn_summary: 波兰艺术家Maria Ka在发现家族犹太根源后，全身心投入意第绪语创作，这张专辑将电子节奏与朋克态度贯穿始终，构建出一个完整的意第绪宇宙。从圣赫尔德加的神秘主义到惠特曼的多重包容性，乐评将作品定位在宗教与世俗边界的消融处。专辑表面分为电子与摇滚两条线索，实则以螺旋式的喜悦感统一。开篇曲目在城市电子研磨节拍中唱出宇宙与陆地的想象，而以摇滚手法处理的一曲直接对意第绪语本身的存续展开辩论，回击了对其语言正确性的质疑。评论将其与John Zorn将怪诞与神圣混入犹太实验音乐的审美相提并论，展现出政治介入的女性主义视角与对宏观社会结构的敏锐感知，整体呈现出小众独立厂牌罕见的文化纵深。

items.body: The Visit by cris derksen The Visit isn�t an album built on compromises. The fourth release from Derksen, a Canadian from the North TallCree Reserve on her father�s side, and with a Mennonite lineage from her mother, pushes and cajoles her visions, where it�s the opening, full-throated improvisation of �White Gladis 1� (with singer Jennifer Kreisberg) or the encompassing haunting mood that grows up around �Lyre Birds.� She�s primarily a cellist, one who works across genres; one of the great joys here is it�s impossible to attach any kind of handle to the music. Just as you think you have it nailed down, the next track is something different, as with the the cello and programming of �aabaakwad� which becomes the wordless singing of �New Heya.� The Visit by cris derksen There�s a raw, unfettered beauty to the album, music made with passion and no restraints. There are a couple of songs here, but nothing that conforms to expectations, altering gears and direction, as when the strings and brass that arrive from nowhere to take over �Buffalo Girls.� The Visit by cris derksen But the emotional centrepiece here is �Lyre Birds,� with Derksen�s cello weaving sparely around the shards of spoken words, leading into the fluttering piano arpeggios of �Nice And Clean.� This is an album of surprises, leading down strange lanes and around brilliant corners that offer startling new views. As both composer and musician, Cris Derksen is more than a singular talent; she�s a person with a vision for her music, and she keeps true to it here. The Visit is not an easy listen, but it is eminently satisfying. Find the artist online. items.body: Review by Aussie-Byrd-Brother — Away from his Anekdoten day job and side-projects My Brother The Wind, Kosmogon and Morte Macabre (1998's `Symphonic Holocaust' is a modern masterpiece that reinterprets horror movie themes as dark and moody improvisations), Swedish multi-instrumentalist Nicklas Barker has also dabbled in soundtrack work, and that latter album in many ways paves the way for his work here, 2011's `El �ltimo Fin De Semana', an eerie and evocative ambient and darkly symphonic Mellotron-dominated stunner.The movie, translated as 'Our Last Weekend' and directed by Spanish film-maker Norberto Ramos del Val, is a horror/thriller about a group of friends that arrive at a secluded mansion to spend the weekend, only to discover that the nearby town harbours a sinister secret. That tension and sense of unease is ripe for Barker to interpret as a fever dream of shadowy instrumental fragments and discordant ideas, a collection of gloomy musical passages, rousing themes and droning ambient interludes, featuring a heavy use of Mellotron and vintage keyboards, theremin, cello and violin.Looking at some of the highlights, opener `Celestial Ghost' sets much of the template for the LP - tremulous theremin, sweetly murmuring seductive bass and droning electronic hums that grow in stature around regal mellotron waves that resemble a gothic choir. Reflective yet doomed with an orchestral-like sophistication, it also displays a mournful beauty. `Night Ambience' teases with a gentle and wavering Berlin School-flavoured fuzzy electronic caress ala Ashra's `New Age of Earth' before turning scratchy and malevolent to really get under the skin.`Sisters/Phantasm', one of the loveliest and most delicate melodies of the disc, is oddly embracing, with ringing chimes and gently haunting Mellotron flute before a brooding, powerful reprise and trailing off into sinking reverberations. `Going Home/Ouija's siren-like spectral Mellotron choirs melt away and bleed into dark synth meditations that hover in the air.Despite a manic, senses shredding opening, `By The Shore' actually turns into a fragile piano respite that gets lifted to the heavens on glorious Mellotron wings, and the up-tempo `Chase/Purgatory' sprints with a pulsing dance beat and slithering synth hisses before luring the listener into a quivering Berlin School-like electronic pool. `Grand Finale' holds one of the strongest themes of the LP, a weeping and dreamy Mellotron lament, and, acting as a sobering come-down, closer `Beach Girls' is a jaunty waltzing ditty that feels like a playful wink in the eye at all the horror and torment the listener has just been through!While it perhaps mines similar ground to the legendary horror movie soundtracks from Italian group Goblin, `El �ltimo Fin De Semana' still succeeds as a lugubrious, haunting work, regardless of whether you've seen the movie it's based on or not. Despite several shorter pieces, the album flows seamlessly and never sounds disjointed, and Barker's arrangements here constantly display intelligence, subtlety, sophistication and supreme taste.Four stars.(Hey, for a fun drinking game, why not take a shot for every time the word `Mellotron' appears in this review?)

items.body: Unfortunately, what was alluded to on last week’s podcast has come to pass, with the passing of our friend Rexx Arkana. The sheer number of tributes to him as a friend, colleague, and supporter we’re seeing from folks in the industrial scene around the world says something about the legacy he leaves behind and the mark he made in with the time he had. We’ll miss you, pal. YZBL Eye New Dark, “Backward Through that Door” Jill Sheridan is a familiar voice via her work with Wisconsin synthpop standard bearers Null Device, and her solo project Eye New Dark follows in the same tradition of extremely musical electronic composition and performance. New single “Backward Through that Door” really does highlight Sheridan’s vocal acumen, and especially her ability to sound both grounded and full-bodied and ethereal in equal measure. On top of that, the song is very nicely put together, minimal in ways that bring out the underlying melodies and structures that keep it moving and evolving. Backwards Through That Door by Eye New Dark YZBL, “Patterns” Lana Del Rabies’ Feral Crone Recordings got off to a strong start last year releasing the latest in LDR’s high-concept death industrial work as well as a solo record from ex-Tassel member Ash Barrett. That association continues with Feral Crone reissuing recent work by other ex-Tasselite YZBL and having her sophomore LP on deck. While last year’s tendril dug into dubby and grimy downtempo, this teaser for Hermaphrodite explores sludgy, stuttering industrial metal which brings any number of Broadrick projects to mind. Hermaphrodite by YZBL Devision Redux, “Synchronize (Excubitors remix)” “Synchronize” by Devision Redux was one of our favourite tracks of 2025, both in the club and for personal listening. The union of De/Vision’s Steffen Keth with Daniel Myer to re-envision the former’s music in a more modern electronic style was certainly a treat live when we caught them at Terminus that summer, and the single was just compulsively listenable, maybe even moreso than in its original form, due to the added melancholia in its performance. New remix single for “Synchronize” sticks to the high energy take on the cut throughout in different variations, and we’re quite taken with the Excubitors remix, which brings some euphoric futurepop to the tune. Synchronize Companion Pieces by Devision Redux Zanias, “The Spire (Trakt Null Remix)” Speaking of remixing some of last year’s faves, one might guess that the trance threads brightly woven through Zanias’ Cataclysm would be stressed in any remixing of that record, but the four mixes of “The Spire” which just dropped counters those expectations. Instead, stripped-down, no-nonsense techno holds sway on many of those versions, though the thudding combo of EBM and big beat offered by German newcomer Trakt Null The Spire Remixes by Zanias Balvanera, “Desgaste” It’s been five years since Angentinian darkwavers Balvanera released Course of Action, a record that feels somewhat prescient given how the electro-darkwave sound has propagated in the years since. How the band have or have not adjusted their approach in the last half-decade is unknown, but first single from Hasta tocar el fondo vacío del lenguaje shows some intriguing developments; there’s a real focus on twonky, slightly out of key lead sound that amp up the menace, even as the swells of reverb and added layers of percussion make it all feel more manic. Hasta tocar el fondo vacío del lenguaje by Balvanera Dead Voices On Air, “Half-Half” We’ve done our best to stay abreast of the torrent of activity from within the Dead Voices On Air camp over the last few years, but between new, collaborative, and archival releases coming fast and furious, that’s no small task. Thankfully, the continued association between Mark Spybey’s longstanding project and Re:Mission has led to a new merch hub collecting the last decade-plus of that work, just in time for this teaser from the forthcoming mothcomma LP. It’s tough to tell if the moments of high drama and bombast which punctuate some classically harmonious Spybey drones are an indicator of things to come, or simply befitting the last track on the record. mothcomma by dead voices on air The post Tracks: July 6th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Chicago dark synth / industrial artist TATV GRAL returns to Side-Line.com with the exclusive video premiereof the DSTR remix of ‘Treachery’, launching alongside the four-track Treachery remix EP. While the original single explores the collision of opposing archetypal forces through a contemporary industrial and dark electronic lens, the remix EP extends the work in another direction, bringing together four distinct interpretations of the song: the original single version produced by William Faith, alongside reinterpretations by DSTR (Daniel Myer of Haujobb), Tweaker (Chris Vrenna of NIN), and fellow Chicago industrial outfit [melter]. Together, they gradually revealed an unexpected narrative to TATV GRAL’s Allen Addington only after the project was complete. Discussing the DSTR remix, Addington says: “I asked Daniel to find something in the song I hadn’t expressed myself – a different vantage on it. He pitched my voice down until it felt like I was speaking through a mask and built the track around a sense of searching rather than arrival. It also felt fitting, given Haujobb’s own homage to Front 242’s ‘Headhunter’ video on ‘We Must Wait’ featuring Jean-Luc De Meyer. Daniel already works within that lineage of one generation nodding to the last. It was only once I had all the remixes back that I recognized a narrative running through them alongside my original. DSTR is the search. [melter]’s mix is the extreme of the moment itself. Tweaker’s is the reflective aftermath. I didn’t consciously plan that arc. It revealed itself only after all the remixes were finished, as though each artist had uncovered a different aspect of the same song. I’m hoping to make two more videos to complete that story.” That same sense of continuity informed the accompanying video, which relocates the song from the symbolic interior spaces of the original clip into Chicago’s historic industrial landscape. Rather than using the city simply as a backdrop, Addington approached it as part of the visual and cultural lineage that shaped the music itself. “I shot it in Bridgeport neighbourhood of Chicago, where I live – the same industrial corridors Front Line Assembly used for ‘Isolate’ and KMFDM for ‘Vogue.’ It’s WAX TRAX! territory. Those same streets have appeared recently in Batman films, which says something about how this city’s decay keeps getting recast as myth. I wanted to uncover the history still present in that landscape – the industrial current that’s been there all along. All the glitch work is hand-built too: no plugins, no AI. Four bars might mean 64 individually designed frames, one at a time. That’s a small homage to where this graphic language actually comes from – hands cutting and layering images long before anyone had a filter to do it for them.” Tatv Gral’s ‘Treachery’ DSTR remix and the ‘Treachery EP’ The “Treachery EP” runs four tracks: the original “Treachery”, the DSTR remix by Daniel Myer, a remix by Chicago act [melter], and a version by Tweaker, the project of Chris Vrenna. The DSTR remix carries the video premiering here. Tatv Gral self-released the original “Treachery” single in June 2026, produced by William Faith at 13 Studio in Chicago. Treachery EP by Tatv Gral About Tatv Gral Tatv Gral is the solo project of Allen Addington, a multimedia artist based in Chicago, Illinois, active since the mid-1990s. The project mixes dark synth and industrial electronics with themes drawn from archetypal psychology and a queer leather aesthetic. Addington issued the debut “The Chase” in May 2019, followed by “Chiron” in June 2019, “Soul Divine” in March 2020 and “Noncommittal Grey” in March 2023. In March 2025 Tatv Gral appeared as a guest at the release show for The Funeral March‘s final album “It All Falls Apart”, alongside [melter] and William Faith. The “Treachery” single arrived in June 2026, and the “Treachery EP” now gathers it with the DSTR, [melter] and Tweaker remixes, led by the Daniel Myer video premiering on Side-Line.
items._cn_summary: 芝加哥暗潮工业艺人TATV GRAL发布'Treachery'四轨混音EP，原版由William Faith制作，另收录Haujobb成员Daniel Myer（DSTR）、Nine Inch Nails成员Chris Vrenna（Tweaker）及芝加哥同团[melter]的三支混音。Addington在采访中表示，邀请DSTR对人声进行降调处理，营造'隔面具发声'的疏离感，并围绕'寻找而非抵达'的概念重构曲目。整体混音EP呈现出一条创作者未事先规划的叙事弧线：DSTR代表探索阶段，[melter]代表极端当下，Tweaker代表反思余波。配套MV在芝加哥Bridgeport工业区实地取景，该区域曾出现于Front Line Assembly和KMFDM的MV中，延续了Wax Trax!厂牌的工业视觉谱系。视频中的故障视觉全部手工逐帧构建，未使用任何AI或插件，以致敬实验影像的剪贴传统。

items.body: Band: Bekor Qilish | Album: Consecrated Abysses of Dread | Genre: Avant-garde metal | Bandcamp The new album from one-man Italian experimental metal act Bekor Qilish sees a further refinement and evolution in the act’s sound. Black metal is still at the root of what he’s doing here, but there is a lot more at play. Riffs are bizarre and ultra-technical. This constant oscillation can be exciting and lead to some fantastic juxtapositions. At the same time, though, it can also come off as disjointed or unfocused. There is a lot to like on this record, but I think Bekor Qilish’s music works best in the format of a slightly-shorter EP. Score: 78/100 Band: Different Light | Album: Binary Suns (Part 2 – Alternate Reality) | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp Different Light is back with part two of their Binary Suns project, six years after releasing part one. Overall, it’s fine. It’s relatively sunny, piano-heavy prog that’s rooted in the 1990s. There is some good occasional crunch, and the vocal performance is strong. Certain passages are maybe a little cheesy for my taste, and transitions between the sub-sections of the suites can occasionally be a little awkward. But if you like Spock’s Beard and crave more Spock’s Beard-sounding music, this is a pretty decent choice. Score: 74/100 Band: Dionysiaque | Album: La Tourbe Des Rêves | Genre: Experimental doom metal | Bandcamp French band Dionysiaque’s sophomore record might just be the most daring and forward-thinking doom metal record I’ve heard. Doom is not often a genre that leans too hard into progressive or experimental ways of writing or playing, but this act shows the potential of this marriage. Riffs are crushing, melodic, and melancholy; and the vocals are dramatic and emotive. The playing is technical and flashy, with drums tumbling, bass snarling, and guitars slicing and shredding where more orthodox doom acts would be content to simply trundle along. Dionysiaque effortlessly folds in black, thrash, and even folk elements alongside their more experimental excursions. Score: 90/100 Band: Mors Verum | Album: Canvas | Genre: Avant-garde metal | Bandcamp Canadian death metallers Mors Verum put forward a dense, challenging, and rewarding 30-minute release on Canvas. Riffs on this are dissonant and coarse, often lending a hazy aura to the whole affair. The band deftly alternates between speedy passages that scour the listener and slower moments where they occasionally dip into more melodic passages. The five songs on this EP gradually unfold in odd, tangled ways which are very satisfying. Score: 85/100 Band: Phideaux | Album: Automoto Animus | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp Phideaux is one of my favorite progressive rock acts, so it pains me to say this, but Automoto Animus is not very good. I’ve been struggling to articulate exactly why this isn’t resonating with me, and I think the best explanation I can come up with is that this record feels somewhat small. Phideaux’s best work (Infernal, Snowtorch, Doomsday Afternoon) has always been grand and epic and sweeping. That sense of scale and scope simply isn’t here on this record.  There are flashes of Phideaux’s usual brilliance, but one of the biggest problems here is that many of the songs feel quite same-y. Most of the songs are about four minutes long and led by bouncy piano with some often-schlocky pop elements. There’s a sense of sterility to a lot of this album. Even the closing 14-minute epic is something of a let-down. It ends strong, but the first nine minutes or so feel like an extension of the preceding compositions. Score: 55/100 Band: Stimmerman | Album: Challenging Music for Difficult People | Genre: Progressive rock, Avant-prog | Bandcamp This album delivers what’s advertised on the tin. The music is weird, full of off-kilter rhythms, atypical chords, and wonky melodies. Stimmerman also blends strains of jazz, metal, alt-rock, and more into a dense and thorny record. Despite all this it’s undeniable that the music here is fun and strangely infectious. The band covers a lot of territory in less than 35 minutes, but it holds together and delivers something that’s greater than the sum of its parts. Score: 82/100

items._cn_summary: 本期涵盖五张前卫金属与实验金属新作。意大利单人计划 Bekor Qilish 在黑金属根基上加入大量超技术化、怪异的变拍节奏，频繁切换造成碎片感，篇幅过长削弱了整体凝练度。法国乐队 Dionysiaque 的第二张专辑被评价为最具胆识的实验厄运金属，将碾压式的旋律吉他与戏剧性人声结合，融入了黑金属、激流甚至民谣元素，鼓击与贝斯展现出强烈的技术张力。加拿大 Mors Verum 的 EP 以不和谐、粗粝的吉他音墙构建朦胧氛围，在疾速段落与缓慢的旋律展开间交替纠缠。来自意大利的不同之光与 Phideaux 则代表传统九十年代钢琴前卫摇滚，前者有稳定的演唱与偶尔的失重感，后者被指过于平淡、缺乏往昔作品的宏大叙事。整体来看，Dionysiaque 与 Mors Verum 在实验边界上走得最远，而两张前卫摇滚作品更偏复古稳妥路线。

items._cn_summary: 这是一张由DJ Michel Isorinne为法国独立厂牌716lavie制作的混音作品，收录了27首来自不同艺术家的曲目，时长77分钟。曲目跨越多个流派，从Bo Hansson的民谣氛围到Coil的工业实验，从Lee Gamble的IDM解构到Alessandro Cortini的模块合成器声响，从Infinity Frequencies的暗潮氛围到Dead Can Dance的新世纪古典。混音将ambient、drone、experimental electronic、dark ambient等元素编织在一起，形成一段连绵的听觉旅程，体现了DJ对地下实验音乐场景的广泛涉猎与独到品味。选曲涵盖多位当代实验音乐人，如Andrew Chalk、Russian Tsarlag、Viktor Sjöberg等，搭配Can、Coil、Dead Can Dance等经典作品，在新旧之间建立对话。该混音作品信息量丰富，但缺乏深入的评论文字，仅作为曲目列表呈现。

items.body: Last year we were introduced to the Ibiza-based NGO MusicForTheSea through Coco Francavilla’s liquid re-oceaning. This year the imprint’s second release was also unveiled on United Nations World Oceans Day, and celebrates the ocean while drawing essential attention to conservation efforts. Tidal Shifts – Reimagine, an outgrowth of an event in Nice, is a collaborative effort among field recordists, composers, and visual artists, incorporating copious underwater recordings from the Strait of Gibraltar captured by the Institute of Marine Research of the University of Cádiz. These recordings lie at the heart of the release, calling one’s ears ever back to the sounds of the sea. IDRA eases us gently into the ocean, beginning at the shore; the waves lap beside twinkling electronics and placid keys. Considering how many ambient tracks from Ibiza have showcased the sound of waves, it’s amazing that so few are this intentional; instead of mere background or sound effect, they are the music’s reason to exist. The soundings of Oora introduce the human element, studying the health of the ecosystem; the waves are louder, as is the rolling of the hull. This is the sound of research rather than intrusion, evidence of scientists hard at work. The “Tides at Bay of Fundy” are the world’s highest, yielding real-time evidence of glacial melt and climate change. As the music grows more active, one can imagine the tide rising, quicker and higher than expected, a parable for the planet’s possible fate. At the very end, there is only the sound of water, along with the sounding instrument; the music has abruptly recessed. Whalesong launchhes Vito Gatto‘s “Introimmersion,” wrapping the listener in a watery blanket. Cascades of keys pass by like schools of fish. Brass enters in the second minute, along with the crackle of what may be brine shrimp. The implication is of something dark and enormous; the question is, benign or threatening? Is this simply the shadow of a passing whale, or the longer shadow cast by the Great Pacific Garbage Patch? The closing “Indigo Reverie” is a collaboration between Kazuya Nagaya and Coco Francavilla, the former fresh from the release of Lumina. During this contemplative piece, one may indeed become lost in one’s thoughts, dreaming of the ocean and weekends by the sea. But to only do so is to miss the point. 15% of the world’s population lives by a coastline, while three times that number visit every summer. The coastline – as well as the health of the sea – is endangered, as are the lives of those who live in and around it. Tidal Shifts may sound comforting, but its intent is to unsettle, or at the very least to motivate. The beauty of “Indigo Reverie” is that it grows like a coral reef; but the music seems always fragile, a reminder that without care, even the most durable facets of life can disintegrate. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: ambient / field recording / experimental electronic / environmental sound art
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Ibiza海洋保护NGO MusicForTheSea发行，核心素材来自直布罗陀海峡的丰富水下录音，由加的斯大学海洋研究所实地采集，构成了一件聚焦海洋保护的环境声音艺术品。作品从海岸环境声逐步引入人与研究的痕迹，浪涌与船体声响交织成为可听化的科学调查证据。整体以氛围电子为基底，融入键盘、铜管与颗粒质感，鲸鱼鸣唱段落通过层层叠置的键盘营造深海沉浸感，暗示庞大而未知的暗流——是鲸的阴影还是海洋垃圾带的隐喻。终曲以珊瑚礁式的缓慢生长结构呈现脆弱之美，表面上宁静舒适，实则以听觉语言传递海洋生态危机与气候变迁的紧迫信号。作品将田野录音、环境声学与氛围电子熔为一体，目的不仅在于审美，更在于唤醒与不安。

items.body: Now You Exist gives me hope that maybe 2018 was not the last time we heard from The Field, because perhaps 2026 won’t be either. In all seriousness, this seems to be a proper comeback in a year of proper comebacks. This EP will not disappoint any longtime fan, but maybe it’s only the beginning of a new era for Willner, who hopefully hasn’t run out of ink—or MIDI tracks. The Field as you may have always known him Now You Exist by The Field   It has been eight years since The Field last published music—not just new music, but any music at all. There had been complete silence, or at least it seemed that way, because I repeatedly looked up any article, interview, or anything on social media that could convince me this man was still alive, and I ended up finding nothing—but maybe it was just me. No live performances, no announcements anywhere, absolutely nothing. Turns out… he is still alive! Not only that, he’s also got some new music with him. Seeing the announcement of this release was almost a shock for me. I initially thought it was some batch of old material that Kompakt (the pillar of leftfield techno under which all of The Field‘s work was published) had managed to unearth. But no, this is genuinely new The Field. Also new is the label, as Now You Exist has been published by Studio Barnhus; if you wonder why that is, you can read the recent article in The Guardian, which explains why this label is the sole reason for this rebirth. Also surprising is the cover, which ends the tradition of all his releases following the same visual template—with the exception of another EP, 2007’s Sound of Light. It is a rebirth in every way, and oh, how lucky we are to witness it. I will first say that Axel Willner‘s debut album, From Here We Go Sublime, is one of my favorite records, period. When I first listened to it some years ago, it blew my mind as to what techno and trance could become when a stroke of genius occurs, so much so that I wouldn’t really dare call it an EDM album in any way. Since then, his whole catalogue has had a grasp on me, and I was let down by the fact that he had seemingly disappeared before I even discovered his music. Now You Exist is a release that brightened not only my day, but my entire month. The opposite of a jack of all trades :: This EP is The Field as you may have always known him. It merges techno beats with atmospheric elements, while trance and psychedelia influences are present throughout. The Field thus proves himself to be the opposite of a jack of all trades. That magical blend of looped, chopped-up vocal samples over ethereal techno was deeply missed, as no one else can replicate this style. It feels as fresh as ever for exactly that reason. There are, however, some interesting aspects about this EP. First is the opening tune, “In Our Dreams,” which is a rare track featuring, I believe, live vocals instead of samples. It is a wonderfully psychedelic cut in which the drums are introduced very shyly, allowing the vocals to shine at first; it gradually shifts from a somewhat ambient piece into an entrancing techno journey and is certainly one of his most unique tracks. A more classic sound is found in the next two tracks, “333 706” and “Hey Baby.” I’m particularly fond of the latter, as it’s the track that most closely resembles a trance song. The last two pieces are even better, and among The Field‘s best material overall, I’d say. “Another Day” is a surprisingly melodic track that barely resembles techno, leaning more toward downtempo. It’s another psychedelic number, extremely relaxed and hazy, though its type of distortion appears throughout most of the EP. The closing title track is a very classic icy techno tune with stuttering vocal chops; the hi-hats, specifically, have that unmistakable Field touch that makes this track instantly recognizable as one of his—and one I’m especially keen on. Now You Exist gives me hope that maybe 2018 was not the last time we heard from The Field, because perhaps 2026 won’t be either. In all seriousness, this seems to be a proper comeback in a year of proper comebacks. This EP will not disappoint any longtime fan, but maybe it’s only the beginning of a new era for Willner, who hopefully hasn’t run out of ink—or MIDI tracks. Originally published on Rate Your Music and republished here with permission. Now You Exist is available on Studio Barnhus. [Bandcamp] Now You Exist by The FieldThe post The Field :: Now You Exist (Studio Barnhus) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: The Field 八年沉寂后携 EP《Now You Exist》回归，发表于瑞典独立厂牌 Studio Barnhus。Axel Willner 延续其标志性风格：将循环切碎的人声采样叠加于氛围化 techno 节奏之上，融入迷幻与 trance 元素，编织出催眠般的声场。开场曲《In Our Dreams》罕见采用真人演唱而非采样处理，增添迷幻质感。这张作品打破其所有封面统一的视觉传统，从厂牌到美学皆属新生。乐评将其首张专辑《From Here We Go Sublime》视为现代 techno 与 trance 融合的典范之作，而本张 EP 延续了那种将循环人声碎片漂浮于空灵 techno 律动之上的独特手法，乐评人认为这种无人能复制的风格在八年后依然新鲜如初。整体保持在 Willner 既有的声音语言框架内，未见大幅突破，但作为长期缺席后的归来之作，对熟悉其美学的听众而言仍具吸引力。

items.body: The inclusion of the original album version closes the circle, reaffirming the strength of a composition capable of surviving such radical reinterpretation. Not merely a remix package, but a study in how distinctive source material can continue evolving without losing its identity. Functional and exploratory; club-focused yet resistant to conformity Few contemporary producers inhabit techno’s established language with the confidence and individuality of Nathan Fake. His work is built from familiar materials: piston-driven 909s, acid-suggestive basslines, vast synth architectures, and melodies that gather momentum with almost unbearable patience. Yet what continues to distinguish Fake is his refusal to settle into genre orthodoxy. Every element feels recognizably techno, but arranged according to a logic entirely his own. The result is music that is simultaneously functional and exploratory; club-focused yet resistant to conformity. It recalls the atmosphere surrounding the seminal Lost parties of Steve Bicknell—serious, immersive, and utterly committed to the dancefloor experience. Originally lifted from Evaporator, Fake‘s celebrated attempt to distil decades of dancefloor immersion into a form of radiant “daytime techno,” “Hypercube” now returns through a collection of remixes that illuminate different facets of its design. Fake‘s own “Hard Version” strips away any remaining daylight and drives directly into the small hours, intensifying the original’s pressure without sacrificing its emotional gravity. Taut, focused, and devastatingly effective. Basile3 contributes the collection’s most thrilling mutation​, transforming the track into a fractured machine-funk exercise where rhythms buckle, pivot, and reassemble around the original motif. Electro currents ripple beneath the surface, lending the track a sense of restless momentum and ecstatic instability. Mac Seldom takes a rougher route, locking into broken rhythms and low-slung tek-funk mechanics, allowing vocal fragments and subterranean bass pressure to collide in gloriously unruly fashion. Tukan, meanwhile, embraces escalation, preserving much of the source before unleashing a colossal white-noise crescendo that feels less like a breakdown than a controlled systems failure. The inclusion of the original album version closes the circle, reaffirming the strength of a composition capable of surviving such radical reinterpretation. Not merely a remix package, but a study in how distinctive source material can continue evolving without losing its identity. Hypercube is available on InFiné. items._cn_summary: 这是一张以Nathan Fake单曲《Hypercube》为核心的remix EP，原曲出自其专辑《Evaporator》，被定位为"日光下的techno"。评论围绕多个remix版本展开分析：Fake自己的"Hard Version"剥离了原曲中的日光感，将声音推向深夜，强化了原有的情绪张力与压力感；Basile3的版本将其解构为碎片化的machine-funk，电流感暗流涌动，节奏不断折叠重构；Mac Seldom采用broken rhythm与低沉的低音机械，呈现粗粝的tek-funk质感；Tukan则在保留原曲结构的基础上引入了大规模的白噪声渐强，制造出接近系统失控般的临界体验。原曲被保留作为收尾，验证了这首作品在不同手法下的可塑性。整体评价聚焦于作品如何在techno的既定语言框架内，通过多种remix视角展现声音设计的多面性，而非单纯的舞曲功能化处理。

items.body: Review by tszirmay — From dual paradises (also known locally as Arizona and California) comes this hefty collaboration between my good friend/ multi-instrumentalist Tenk van Dool and master percussor Paul Sears, with a little help from assorted friends. I still enjoy revisiting the Temple of Switches album , which had the advantage of prepping me for this 'primal instinct' example of musical lunacy. Since I despise the very notion of labelling (it's only good for food products!), let us limit ourselves to state for the record that Tenk and Paul navigate in some inventive sonic realms that may include a wide variety of endearing as well as bludgeoning sequences, scales and sequins, also known in more conventional terms as jazz-rock, improvisations and psychedelia. The solos are instinctive, the mood cerebral and the expounding virtues emit impeccable originality. Eleven vignettes , astutely opened windows within a collapsing universe."King Koln" has nothing to do with the Rhine valley but easily provides some mechanical kling-klang that would confound the remaining Kraftwerk crew (RIP Florian), a steel foundry of puncturing guitar vacillations, billowing synthesized smokestacks, with punctuating and puncturing drum tutelage. Lovely noise. The Teutonic mood is maintained on "Cappy's Sledge" featuring seething vocals from Heinrich the 'fecal house cleaner' and Klopfen 'the pigmy dwarf', somehow recalling some Zomby Woof Italian-American, surely a modern version of the Flo and Eddie skit, but with severe Gothic overtones. Thankfully, the Van Dool axe solo is a pungent blitzkrieg that does the trick. What better way to comb one's bald spot than with "Head Scratcher", a velvety scrutiny of tasty twirls on the guitar, spiced by keyboard sorcery and the kind of percussive backbone that comes straight out of a sweaty jazz cavern somewhere downtown. How about a cinematic survey on the late-night lizards roaming the urban decay well after midnight on "1am Geary Street", replete with Courtney Odom hushing her vocalizations! Dazed and confused, tired and spent, a "yes I'm lonely, wanna die" mood, exacerbated by some quarrelsome electric guitar frittering, bickering drum slaps and splashes and some nighttime dissonance to help with the paranoid insomnia!Epic track time with an 8-and-a-half-minute romper "Land of the Free", a perfect and completely improvised basal platform for the choo-choo train to unload some progressive passengers at Union Station. Steve Mitchell guests on guitars and bass, while Ruben Riera blows forcefully on pan flute as well as woodwinds. The ambient drowsy nature is intoxicating, with a real bludgeoning of the senses without resorting to any violent interactions. Tenk brings out his African bongos to complement Paul's fluctuating pulsations, and a merry time is had by all. Really enjoyable, in a semi-masochistic manner."Tandem Trike to Tiburon" may hint at Spanish-speaking sharks riding bicycles in some obscure way but comes across as almost accessible after the previous medicated bliss. A relatively immediate groove is put in place, an unblushing piano shuffle, with outright jazz implications and a viscous bass travelogue roaming unfettered. Affectionately warped. "Tribledation" keeps the onus on the black and white ivories (Tenk is a real talent, I will admit!) and could have lasted a bit longer. But connected with the next two brief pieces, I get the idea, as the pace flows rather concisely!I have no idea (nor do I need to know) who "Katie and Nathalie" are but it's another vocal piece that has Clara Belle Hembree warbling in a wistful style that exudes heavy psychedelics, I guess it's hard to get the California dreaming thingy out of one's mind. As such, the track is a consummate slice of fluffy genius, with a deliriously perfect sax solo (yeah, baby!), slithering guitar flickers and adhesive melodies to boot. Me gusta muchissimo!The album terminates its course in some detached realm, where "Souls" find their eternal rest, a finale that sweeps all the turmoil away in a sweep of delicate sound and distant thunder. Guitars, keys, bass and drums settle the score.This was fun.4 basic instincts

items._cn_summary: 这是一位多乐器演奏家Tenk van Dool与鼓手Paul Sears合作的专辑，融合爵士摇滚、即兴与迷幻元素，呈现出一种'原始冲动'式的音乐狂想。专辑由十一首小品组成，风格多变：机械感十足的工业律动、哥特式人声合唱、爵士洞穴般的吉他独奏、午夜都市的电影感氛围，以及长达八分半钟的完全即兴之作。制作中邀请多位客座乐手贡献木管、潘笛、非洲邦戈等音色，营造出层次丰富的声场。评论强调其'本能性独奏'与'理智情绪'并存的特质，以及无可挑剔的原创性，乐手间的即兴对话构成全作核心张力。

items.body: Texan artist Rona Rougeheart has been active as SINE for several years, releasing music on labels such as Re:Mission, Emergency Hearts, and Negative Gain Productions. With “La Mordre”, however, she takes a major step forward, marking her debut release on Metropolis Records. “La Mordre” is a captivating musical experience—one that stands out for both its originality and its consistently high quality. Rather than sounding like a derivative of better-known acts, SINE has developed a distinctive sonic identity all her own. Her music seamlessly blends elements of Minimal-Electro, Dark-Pop, Industrial, and even touches of Hip-Hop into a cohesive and compelling whole. The album is built around deep, resonant bass tones, slow and seductive rhythms, and Rougeheart’s semi-spoken, sensual vocal delivery. Together, these elements create an atmosphere that is both unsettling and intensely alluring, balancing darkness with an undeniable sense of intimacy. From beginning to end, “La Mordre” delivers one outstanding track after another. Its hypnotic grooves and provocative mood make it the perfect soundtrack for an underground fetish club or a late-night Industrial dancefloor. This is an album that dares to be different—and succeeds with remarkable confidence. (Rating:8½). SINE released “La Mordre” in May 2026, a ten-track album that gathers four earlier singles alongside six new recordings. Listen to “Succumb To Me”: Succumb To Me by SINE About SINE SINE is the solo project of Rona Rougeheart, a drummer, vocalist, producer, and multi-instrumentalist based in Austin, Texas. Rougeheart uses the term “Electronic Boom” to describe the project’s sound, which blends sub-bass, beats, and industrial elements with lyrics that incorporate sarcasm, humour, and social commentary. The project’s early releases appeared on Austin’s eMERGENCY heARTS label. SINE’s 2021 album “Desire, Denial and Paramania” was released on 7 October 2021 and featured collaborations with Curse Mackey, producer Sean Beavan (Nine Inch Nails, 3Teeth), and vocalist Chris Connelly (Pigface, Revolting Cocks). The album also included a Meat Beat Manifesto remix by Jack Dangers. In January 2022, SINE released a remix of “Attack” by Adrian Sherwood on eMERGENCY heARTS, and in August 2022 issued the EP “Mantis 2” on the same label. SINE signed to Metropolis Records ahead of the 2024 album “Luxuria”, released on 19 January 2024. That record was produced by Claus Larsen of Leæther Strip and included the single “From Beyond” featuring Leæther Strip. Over the course of her career, Rougeheart has collaborated with Adrian Sherwood, Meat Beat Manifesto, Clan of Xymox, Chris Connelly, Mark Pistel, Andee Blacksugar (KMFDM, Blondie), Xiu Xiu, and the late Mark Stewart of The Pop Group. “La Mordre,” her second Metropolis release, arrives roughly two years after “Luxuria” and marks a step into a longer, more expansive album format.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑融合了极简电子、暗潮、工业和暗黑流行的元素，同时融入少量嘻哈节奏感。整张作品以深沉的贝斯音色为核心，缓慢而具诱惑力的律动层叠推进，配以半吟诵式的感性人声，形成在黑暗中交织亲密感与不安感的独特氛围。十首曲目各具张力，从头到尾保持一致的高水准与连贯性，适合地下俱乐部及深夜舞场场景。该专辑最大的特色在于艺术家建立了完全个人化的声音辨识度，而非模仿既有知名乐队的风格，证明了她在主流厂牌旗下依然保有强烈的独立创作意识。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Alison Cotton 的新专辑延续其标志性的中世纪神秘氛围，将民谣根基与前卫即兴手法相结合。乐器编制以中提琴、管风琴、锤击扬琴与钢琴为核心，新加入鼓、贝斯与合成器拓宽了声场层次。多首作品采一次成型即兴录制，营造出穿越时空的远古感。在编曲上保留 drone 式持续低音作为基底，却在旋律层面展现出接近中世纪圣咏的简洁与肃穆。整张专辑同时是对其 2024 年底去世的父亲的悼念之作，多首曲目流露出丧失与怀念的私人情感，但并未陷入滥情，而是在光暗交替中维持了仪式的庄严与克制。音乐超越类型边界，既非纯古典也非传统民谣，而是一种难以归类的个人化声响表达。
